1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time
     2	
     3	**count stage**
     4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library and prints its errors: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total, the checker count, counts the errors up to each component's first error.
     5	
     6	The code of this area is in these directories:
     7	
     8	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
     9	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
    10	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
    11	
    12	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
    13	
    14	## What the two paths share
    15	
    16	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
    17	
    18	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
    19	- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
    20	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
    21	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
    22	
    23	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
    24	
    25	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
    26	
    27	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
    28	
    29	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
    30	
    31	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
    32	
    33	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
    34	
    35	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
    36	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
    37	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
    38	
    39	It also refuses a function, method, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause of its own, and a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose `extends` entry has a `where` clause. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).
    40	
    41	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
    42	
    43	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
    44	
    45	## What the code generator does
    46	
    47	`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.
    48	
    49	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
    50	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
    51	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
    52	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
    53	
    54	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
    55	
    56	## The run time
    57	
    58	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
    59	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.
    60	
    61	## Natives
    62	
    63	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
    64	
    65	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
    66	
    67	## Traps of the compiled path
    68	
    69	- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
    70	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
    71	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
    72	
    73	## The `fortress` commands
    74	
    75	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
    76	
    77	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
    78	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
    79	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
    80	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
    81	
    82	## Running
    83	
    84	    cd ProjectFortress
    85	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    86	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    87	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
    88	
    89	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
    90	
    91	- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
    92	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.
    93	
    94	## Before an edit
    95	
    96	Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
    97	
    98	- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
    99	
   100	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'
   101	
   102	- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.
   103	
   104	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'
   105	
   106	- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.
   107	
   108	## Testing an edit here
   109	
   110	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:
   111	
   112	      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
   113	      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
   114	      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
   115	      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
   116	      bin/fortress run P
   117	
   118	  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
   119	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).
   120	
   121	## The checker's time
   122	
   123	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
   124	
   125	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about a minute. It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
   126	
   127	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
   128	
   129	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
   130	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
   131	
   132	A node's hash starts from its class's name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks or a union's members, moves only where the change itself moves it. Such a move is a difference: keep the old order, or report the difference, as for any other.
   133	
   134	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
   135	
   136	The timing is a smoke test. It is there to catch a slowdown of several times, or of orders of magnitude: a change that makes the checker three times slower must show. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
   137	
   138	If you change the checker:

1	# The library
     2	
     3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
     4	
     5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
     6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
     7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
     8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
     9	
    10	## How loops and reductions call the library
    11	
    12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
    13	
    14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
    15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
    16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
    17	
    18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
    19	
    20	## The curator's decisions on the library
    21	
    22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
    23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
    24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
    25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. If the generators and the body do not fix the element type, write it, also where a declared type receives the value: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
    26	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
    27	
    28	## Designing a change
    29	
    30	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
    31	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
    32	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
    33	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
    34	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
    35	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
    36	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
    37	- A new native is a Java class under `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"), so it is an edit of walk's Java too.
    38	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.
    39	
    40	## Editing
    41	
    42	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.

1	# The interpreter (walk)
     2	
     3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
     4	
     5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
     6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
     7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
     8	- `glue/`: the natives.
     9	
    10	## How walk evaluates a program
    11	
    12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
    13	
    14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
    15	
    16	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.
    17	
    18	## Where a fix of walk belongs
    19	
    20	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
    21	
    22	- coercion;
    23	- chained comparisons;
    24	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
    25	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
    26	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
    27	
    28	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.
    29	
    30	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.
    31	
    32	## What walk checks
    33	
    34	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
    35	
    36	At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It refuses:
    37	
    38	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it loads the pair only if the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the return-type rule hold on their declared domains, except in the cases that `revival-changes.md` lists. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes, so such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail. `revival-changes.md`, "Walk's check of two generic declarations", defines the declared domain and lists those cases.
    39	- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`) in a type that provides both.
    40	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
    41	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses.
    42	- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
    43	- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
    44	  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
    45	  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.
    46	
    47	  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.
    48	
    49	So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:
    50	
    51	- adds an overload;
    52	- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
    53	- adds an `override` that overrides nothing.
    54	
    55	`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
    56	
    57	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
    58	
    59	## Natives
    60	
    61	The library binds each of walk's natives by a string in its `.fss` files: `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")`. The classes are in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them. `import java`, the compiled path's way to bind natives, is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it.
    62	
    63	To raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees, a native throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:
    64	
    65	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    66	    return new FortressError(f);
    67	
    68	A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, a division by zero too.
    69	
    70	## Running a program
    71	
    72	    bin/fortress P.fss
    73	
    74	- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
    75	- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
    76	- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
    77	- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
    78	- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
    79	- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
    80	- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.
    81	
    82	## The model program
    83	
    84	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.
    85	
    86	- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
    87	- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.
